documentNotes.title: Read once more before you start your work
documentNotes.statement:
**General note.** Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may make no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): «impossible situation – ситуация невозможна». Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

**Data from the tables** (Planetary data, stars, constants, etc.) may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «Да-Yes» or «Нет-No» have to be written in English or Russian.

Do not forget that in clean copy you should write solutions **only on even (left) pages**. The odd (right) pages will be used by your team leader to translate solutions into English and also to emphasize your thoughts in solutions.

| EVEN PAGE / ЧЁТНАЯ СТРАНИЦА | ODD PAGE / НЕЧЁТНАЯ СТРАНИЦА |
|---|---|
| Текст решения. Text of solution. Текст решения. Text of solution. Текст решения. Text of solution. | × |

documentNotes.title: Ещё раз прочитайте перед началом работы
documentNotes.statement:
**Общее замечание.** Не исключено, что не во всех задачах вопросы поставлены корректно. Некоторые вопросы (возможно, главный вопрос задачи, возможно – подвопрос) могут не иметь смысла. В этом случае следует написать в ответе (по-русски или по-английски): «ситуация невозможна – impossible situation». Естественно, ответ должен быть подкреплён вычислениями или логическими рассуждениями.

**Данные из таблиц** (Солнечная система, звёзды, константы) могут быть использованы в любой задаче.

Ответы «Да-Yes» или «Нет-No» должны быть написаны по-русски или по-английски.

Не забудьте, что в чистовике вы должны писать решения только на чётных (левых) страницах. Нечётные (правые) страницы предназначены для того, чтобы руководитель вашей команды перевёл решения на английский язык и подчеркнул основные мысли решения.

documentNotes.title: Printed discrepancies
documentNotes.statement: The answer key uses 1.34ᵐ for α Centauri B while its data table gives 1.33ᵐ. The summit key invokes brown dwarfs despite the stated A–M main-sequence restriction, and calls an isosceles triangle equilateral. Its printed sin β/2 expressions are preserved. The mirror key says losing K% on transmission despite the statement saying transmitting K%. The eclipse key prints V₃ = V₂ − V_E and L_NS for the along-track width, while nearby prose uses Vφ and L_WE; these are not silently changed. The printed β-2 grading allocations and subtotals are retained.

problems.title: α-1. Double star.
problems.statement: A double star consists of components by all physical characteristics equal to α Centauri A and α Centauri B, which are rotating around the common center of gravity by circular orbits. As observed from the Earth the angular distance between the components varies from $0.17''$ till $2.2''$ with a period of $\tau=39.6$ years. Find the distance to the double star.

solution.statement:
As the components move in circular orbits around their common center of mass, the distance between them does not change. Therefore observed from Earth, the angular distance between them can be changed only due to the fact that we see the orbits of the stars inclined.

The angular distance between the stars becomes maximum ($2.2''$) when the line connecting them is perpendicular to the direction to the Earth (see figure). This situation take place twice during one period $T_\Sigma$ of rotating the stars, so $T_\Sigma=2\tau=79.2$ years. The total mass of the system $M_\Sigma$ (in solar masses) is equal to $M_\Sigma=1.11M_\odot+0.93M_\odot=2.04M_\odot$.

In the system of units $M_\odot$ – year – au the Kepler's third law may be expressed as
$$a^3/T^2\mathbin{\cdot}M=1.$$
Therefore, in this binary system the semimajor axis of the relative orbit (in this case, the distance between the components) will be equal to
$$a_\Sigma=(T_\Sigma^2\mathbin{\cdot}M_\Sigma)^{1/3}\approx23.4\ \mathrm{au}.$$
As follows from the problem situation these 23.4 au are visible from the Earth as an angle of $2.2''$, therefore,…

… the distance (in parsecs), at which this double star is located, will be:
$$L=23.4/2.2\approx10.63\ \mathrm{pc}\approx10.6\ \mathrm{pc}.$$
**Answer: about ten and a half parsecs.**

sections.statement:
| Basic criteria | Points |
|---|---:|

| $T_\Sigma=2\tau=79.2$ years | 1 |
| $a_\Sigma=(T_\Sigma^2M_\Sigma)^{1/3}\approx23.4$ au | 2 |
| Understanding relations between a and L (using parallax) | 1 |
| L ≈ 10.5 pc | 2 |

problems.title: β-1. Double star.
problems.statement: A double star consists of components by all physical characteristics equal to α Centauri A and α Centauri B, which are rotating around the common center of gravity by circular orbits. As observed from the Earth the angular distance between the components varies from $0.17''$ till $2.2''$ with a period of $\tau=39.6$ years. Find the apparent magnitude of every component and also their combined magnitude.

solution.statement:
As the components move in circular orbits around their common center of mass, the distance between them does not change. Therefore observed from Earth, the angular distance between them can be changed only due to the fact that we see the orbits of the stars inclined.

The angular distance between the stars becomes maximum ($2.2''$) when the line connecting them is perpendicular to the direction to the Earth (see figure). This situation take place twice during one period $T_\Sigma$ of rotating the stars, so $T_\Sigma=2\tau=79.2$ years. The total mass of the system $M_\Sigma$ (in solar masses) is equal to $M_\Sigma=1.11M_\odot+0.93M_\odot=2.04M_\odot$.

In the system of units $M_\odot$ – year – au the Kepler's third law may be expressed as
$$a^3/T^2\mathbin{\cdot}M=1.$$
Therefore, in this binary system the semimajor axis of the relative orbit (in this case, the distance between the components) will be equal to
$$a_\Sigma=(T_\Sigma^2\mathbin{\cdot}M_\Sigma)^{1/3}\approx23.4\ \mathrm{au}.$$
As follows from the problem situation these 23.4 au are visible from the Earth as an angle of $2.2''$, therefore,…

… parallax of the double star equals to
$$p=2.2''/23.4\approx0.094''.$$
(You can also find the distance at which the double star is located, in parsecs
$$L=23.4/2.2\approx10.63\ \mathrm{pc}\approx10.6\ \mathrm{pc}.)$$
By comparing the components with the real α Centauri A and α Centauri B, which have parallax $0.747''$ and magnitudes $-0.01^{\mathrm m}$ and $1.34^{\mathrm m}$, we get:
$$m_1=m_{\alpha\mathrm{CenA}}-5^{\mathrm m}\lg(p/p_{\alpha\mathrm{CenA}})=-0.01^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}\lg(0.747/0.094)=-0.01^{\mathrm m}+4.48^{\mathrm m}\approx4.5^{\mathrm m},$$
$$m_2=m_{\alpha\mathrm{CenB}}-5^{\mathrm m}\lg(p/p_{\alpha\mathrm{CenB}})=1.34^{\mathrm m}+5^{\mathrm m}\lg(0.747/0.094)=1.34^{\mathrm m}+4.48^{\mathrm m}\approx5.8^{\mathrm m}.$$
…
$$\Delta m=+5^{\mathrm m}\lg(L_1/L_{\alpha\mathrm{Cen}})=+5^{\mathrm m}\lg(10.6/1.34)\approx4.49^{\mathrm m}).$$
The total magnitude of the two components will be equal to
$$m_{1+2}=-2.5^{\mathrm m}\lg(10^{-m_1/2.5}+10^{-m_2/2.5})\approx4.2^{\mathrm m}.$$
(One can also first find the total magnitude of both components of α Centauri as
$$m_{\alpha\mathrm{Cen}(A+B)}=-2.5^{\mathrm m}\lg(10^{-m_{\alpha\mathrm{CenA}}/2.5}+10^{-m_{\alpha\mathrm{CenB}}/2.5})\approx-0.28^{\mathrm m},$$
and then add to it the difference of $+4.48^{\mathrm m}$ and get the same $4.2^{\mathrm m}$).

**Answers:** $m_1\approx4.5^{\mathrm m}$, $m_2\approx5.8^{\mathrm m}$, $m_{1+2}\approx4.2^{\mathrm m}$.

problems.title: α-2. Extraterrestrial summit.
problems.statement: Extraterrestrial Bear and Extraterrestrial Penguin living in different planetary systems of our Galaxy, came to a summit organized at the Intercivilizational Space Station (ISS) somewhere in the depths of space, where no one star is visible brighter than $1^{\mathrm m}$. However, it appeared that both the stars, from which planetary systems the Bear and the Penguin came, are visible with the naked eye at the summit (assume the sensitivity of the retina of these extraterrestrial animals to be the same as of humans), and the angular distance between them is equal to $\boldsymbol\beta=30^\circ$.

figures.alt: Original Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with temperature, magnitude and spectral-class scales

solution.statement:
The minimum distance between native stars of Bear and Penguin will be in the case when the distances between these stars and the venue of the summit also will be minimum. At the minimum possible distance that satisfies the conditions of the problem may be brown dwarfs with apparent magnitude of $1^{\mathrm m}$, and absolute one of $16^{\mathrm m}$. Accordingly, the distance to a brown dwarf anyway
$$r=10^{[0.2(m-M+5)]}\approx0.01\ \mathrm{pc}.$$
The distance between two such stars can be found, having considered the equilateral triangle, length of base equal to
$$L=r_B\,2\sin\beta/2$$
$$L=0{,}01\ \mathrm{pc}\times2\sin15^\circ\approx0.005\ \mathrm{pc}\approx1000\ \mathrm{au}.$$
(more precise value here does not make sense).

Answer: **about 0,005 pc or 1000 a.u.**

To find the maximum distance between the stars we have to consider several options, which, however, will be calculated using the maximum distance from the summit to the stars of Penguin or a Bear. In order that the star was as far as possible, observer must see it as a faint object (star of $6^{\mathrm m}$), and it should have high luminosity (the star of the class A0 with an absolute visible magnitude of about $0.5^{\mathrm m}$). Then, using the formula for the absolute magnitude will get:
$$R=10^{[0.2(m-M+5)]}\approx126\ \mathrm{pc}.$$
Now consider two options for a possible maximum distance:

1. We have two different stars: a brown dwarf and a main sequence star of spectral class A. The first one is on minimum possible distance, the second – on highest possible distance. The distance between them is calculated in this case by theorem of cosines:
$$L_\mathrm I=[r^2+R^2-2rR\cos\beta]^{1/2}.$$
If you take the r for a brown dwarf (the value of which we found earlier), due to the small values of r compared to R in the formula $L_\mathrm I$ it can be neglected. And then the distance between stars would actually be equal to the distance from the summit to the star of spectral class A0.

2. If we have two stars of the main sequence of spectral class A, then the distance between them is given by the same theorem of cosines, but in a slightly simplified form:
$$L_\mathrm{II}=R[2(1-\cos\beta)]^{1/2}=2R\sin\beta/2.$$
We get an isosceles triangle while the third side will be less than the first two ($\beta<60^\circ$), this formula will not give the maximum distance. However, when our triangle to turn into an equilateral ($\beta=60^\circ$) and the angle at the apex will continue to increase ($\beta>60^\circ$), the distance between the stars will also increase, which cannot be said about the first the case.

From the task we have the angle $\beta=30^\circ$, so the second of the options considered, we are not automatically perfect. Accordingly, the maximum distance between the stars is approximately 130 pc (more precisely to say here does not make sense).

Answer: **about 130 pc.**

In the context of our problem it is from 0.005 to 0.015 pc or from 1000 au to 3000 au (more precise values here does not make sense).

problems.title: αβ-3. Mirror and plate.
problems.statement:
There is a system, consisting of a plane mirror (100% reflection) and a plane glass plate that transmits K% of the light and reflects the other (100-K)% (this characteristics is the same for the light coming from both the directions). The mirror and plate are parallel and infinite on their right side. An observer is placed at the point O (marked by *) and sees a star with a magnitude $2^{\mathrm m}$ within a cone around direction «A». What magnitude(s) star(s) (if any) would the observer see in a cone near direction «B» that is symmetrical to «A»? Calculate numerical value for K = 50% and K = 5% for each such a star (if any visible) or explain why no stars are visible.

![Mirror and plate, observer O and directions A and B](#mirror-statement)

figures.alt: Mirror and plate, observer O and directions A and B

solution.statement:
The observer sees the combined light from parallel rays A1, A2, A3, A4,.. in the direction B. Every beam AN once passed through the plate (losing K%), then successively reflected from the mirror (without losing intensity) and from plates (each time losing (100-K)% of the light), with N reflections from mirrors and N-1 reflections from the plate.

![Official reflected-ray diagram](#mirror-solution)

As the star is at a very large distance, all the rays AN are coming from the mentioned star $2^{\mathrm m}$. Therefore, the observer sees in the direction “B” a single star, the intensity of which we need to calculate as the sum of the series:
$$P_0k+P_0(1-k)k+P_0(1-k)^2k+P_0(1-k)^3k+P_0(1-k)^4k+P_0(1-k)^5k+\ldots$$
where $P_0$ is the flow of light from the star $2^{\mathrm m}$, and k is the fraction of the transmitted light from the plate (i.e., k = K/100).

The sum of the series $1+(1-k)+(1-k)^2+(1-k)^3+(1-k)^4+(1-k)^5+\ldots$ is equal to 1/k. Accordingly, the sum of our series is
$$P_0k(1+(1-k)+(1-k)^2+(1-k)^3+(1-k)^4+(1-k)^5+\ldots)=P_0k\,1/k=P_0.$$
Paradoxically, the fact! Regardless of the value of K the observer would see the only one star in the direction “B”, and its magnitude is $2^{\mathrm m}$.

So the numerical answer in the both cases: $2^{\mathrm m}$.

problems.title: α-4. Eclipse in USA.
problems.statement: A little more than two months ago, on August 21, 2017 from West to East of the USA territory a total solar eclipse was observed. The middle line of the track of the eclipse is shown schematically on the map. Below are four pictures taken by the Bulgarian-Russian group of observers who were in state of Oregon, through which the Moon’s shadow ran as it shown in Fig.α4. (see separate sheet). The local time (UT −07) of the shots is indicated below each image. By using the data and making calculations, estimate:

figures.alt: Eclipse path map and four original images with local-time labels
Original Oregon eclipse map with numbered shadow positions and full boundary

sections.statement:
Let us analyze the ellipse of the Moon’s shadow on the Earth's surface to calculate the altitude h of the Sun. If the diameter of the Moon's shadow near the Earth is denoted by D, the lengths of these axes equal to:

in the azimuth direction, where the Moon and the Sun are: $A=D/\sin h$,

in the direction perpendicular to this azimuth: $B=D$.

Thus, from these two equations: $\sin h=B/A$.

Measuring lengths of the axes of the shadow “2” on the given map, we get:
$$\sin h=26\ \mathrm{mm}/39\ \mathrm{mm}.$$
$$h=\arcsin(2/3)=41.8^\circ.$$
Answer: about 42°.

*Note. In reality, the height of the Sun during the totality phase in Oregon was from 39° (in the West part) to 45° (in the East part), and in the selected for measurement place “2” it was 41.9°.*

The size of the eclipsing shadow along the central line of the path is the speed of the shadow multiplied by the duration of the total phase, and the difference in the positions of shadows “1” and “2” is the speed of the shadow multiplied by the time that we need to find.

The duration of the totality can be obtained by analyzing pictures 2 and 4. Both of them demonstrate the so-called "diamond ring", a unique phenomenon, lasting a few seconds only. It is seen that images of approximately symmetrical in shape, and were shorted about 3-4 seconds before the second contact and after 3-4 seconds of the third one. In addition, from the fact that the points of the second and the third contacts are almost symmetric, it can be concluded that the Bulgarian-Russian group observed the central eclipse and, therefore, was located about in the middle of the totality path. Thus, it is possible to obtain the totality duration at the middle of the path $\tau=2^{\mathrm m}04^{\mathrm s}$ by calculating the time difference of the dating of these images.

*Note. The above few seconds before the second contact and after the third one is a very delicate moment. It should not be considered an error if a participant will not take it into account and use the value $\tau=2^{\mathrm m}11^{\mathrm s}$.*

Making the necessary measurements on the map, we get:
$$t=\tau\times(42.5\ \mathrm{mm}/30\ \mathrm{mm})=176\ \mathrm s\approx180\ \mathrm s.$$
Answer: about 180 seconds.

*Note. In reality, 180 seconds is the interval between the positions of the shadow on the map.*

problems.title: β-4. Eclipse in USA.
problems.statement: A little more than two months ago, on August 21, 2017 from West to East of the USA territory a total solar eclipse was observed. The middle line of the track of the eclipse is shown schematically on the map. Below are four pictures taken by the Bulgarian-Russian group of observers who were near the West coast, in the state of Oregon, through which the Moon’s shadow ran almost along the latitude $\varphi=45^\circ$. The local time (UT −07) of the shots is indicated below each image. At the moment of totality the Sun was in the South-Eastern part of the sky, in $\chi=59{,}5^\circ$ from the South in azimuth, at an altitude of $h=41.9^\circ$ above the horizon. By using the data and making calculations, estimate:

figures.alt: Eclipse path map and four original images with local-time labels

sections.statement:
At first, we have to calculate the speed of the shadow on the Earth's surface. The speed of the Moon in its synodic movement around the Earth is
$$V_1=2\pi R_\mathrm{moon}/T_\mathrm{moon}=(6.28\cdot384\,400\,000\ \mathrm m)/(29.53\cdot24\cdot60\cdot60\ \mathrm s)=947\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$
The same speed would have the speed of the Moon’s shadow on perpendicular to the Sun direction unmoving surface. To take into account the inclination of the territory of Oregon during the eclipse to the perpendicular unmoving surface, we should divide $V_1$ by the sine of some angle $h_E$, which is defined as
$$h_E=\arctan(\tan h/\sin\chi),$$
where χ is the angle between the direction to the South and the azimuth of the Sun, in our case it is 59,5°.
$$V_2=V_1/\sin h_E=V_1/\sin(\arctan(\tan h/\sin\chi))^\circ=1313\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$
And to take into account moving of the territory of Oregon due to sidereal rotation of the Earth we should substrate synodic (!) speed $V_\varphi$ of a point at latitude $\varphi=45^\circ$ from $V_2$
$$V_\varphi=V_E\cos\varphi=2\pi R_E/T_E\cos\varphi=(6{,}283\cdot6378\,000\ \mathrm m/(24\cdot60\cdot60\ \mathrm s))\cdot0{,}707=328\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$
$$V_3=V_2-V_E=1313\ \mathrm{m/s}-328\ \mathrm{m/s}\approx985\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$
As we consider the pass of the eclipse was going along the geographical parallel, the other corrections should be not taken into account. So the speed of the Moon’s shadow on the territory of Oregon was about 985 m/s, and it is the answer to the first part of the problem.

*Note. The real value of the speed of the shadow in that area was 1001 m/s.*

The size of the eclipsing shadow on the Earth is determined by the projection of the Moon’s shade diameter D of the cone on the Earth's surface. This is usually an ellipse with axes equal to:

in the azimuth direction, where there are the Moon and the Sun: $A=D/\sin h$,

in the direction perpendicular to this azimuth direction: $B=D$.

It is more complicated to calculate the size of the shadow in other directions, but for ellipses with small eccentricities it is possible to use the approximation formula:
$$L=B+(A-B)\cos\alpha,$$
where α is the angle between the direction of measuring and the semi-major axis of the ellipse. The semi-major axis of the ellipse is directed to the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, it is also at an angle χ = 59.5° to the direction of the South in this configuration. One can write the approximate relations for the size of the shadow on the Earth's surface:

…

Substituting the numerical values of the angles, we get:
$$A\approx1.5B,\quad L_\mathrm{NS}\approx1.25B,\quad L_\mathrm{WE}\approx1.43B,\quad L_\mathrm{NS}\approx0.87L_\mathrm{WE}.$$
We need the width of track that is the size of the shadow in the direction perpendicular to the movement of the shadow that is approximately the direction North-South in our case, $L_\mathrm{NS}$. And the size of the shadow in the direction of its movement, $L_\mathrm{WE}$, approximately West-East, can be calculated as the speed of the shadow multiplied by the duration of the total phase of the Eclipse:
$$L_\mathrm{WE}=V\tau,$$
The duration of the totality can be obtained by analyzing pictures 2 and 4. Both of them demonstrate the so-called "diamond ring", a unique phenomenon, lasting a few seconds only. It is seen that images of approximately symmetrical in shape, and were shorted about 3-4 seconds before the second contact and after 3-4 seconds of the third one. In addition, from the fact that the points of the second and the third contacts are almost symmetric, it can be concluded that the Bulgarian-Russian group observed the central eclipse and, therefore, was located about in the middle of the totality path. Thus, it is possible to obtain the totality duration at the middle of the path $\tau=2^{\mathrm m}04^{\mathrm s}$ by calculating the time difference of the dating of these images.

*Note. The above few seconds before the second contact and after the third one is a very delicate moment. It should not be considered an error if a participant will not take it into account and use the value $\tau=2^{\mathrm m}11^{\mathrm s}$.*

Thus, the size of the shadow on the Earth's surface in the direction of its motion is equal to:
$$L_\mathrm{NS}=V_3\tau=985\ \mathrm{m/s}\times2^{\mathrm m}04^{\mathrm s}\approx120\ \mathrm{km},$$
and the size in the perpendicular direction:
$$L_\mathrm{NS}=0{,}87L_\mathrm{WE}=0{,}87\cdot120\ \mathrm{km}\approx105\ \mathrm{km}.$$
Thus, the width of the path of the totality was equal to approximately 105 km.

*Note. The real value of the width of the path in that area was 102 km.*

problems.title: α-5. Whirlpool galaxy.
problems.statement: An imaging observation of Messier object M51, consisted of galaxy NGC 5194 ($\alpha=13^{\mathrm h}29^{\mathrm m}56^{\mathrm s}$, $\delta=+47^\circ13'50''$) and its companion NGC 5195, was made by the 1-m telescope of Weihai Observatory (WHO), on December 25, 2014. The V-band image is shown in Fig.α5. (see separate sheet), the bounding box marks the field of view of the image taken by the telescope (with focal length of 8 meters) and the PI CCD (2048 × 2048, pixel size 13.5 μm × 13.5 μm).

figures.alt: Original M51 image with complete CCD field boundary

sections.title: 5.1. Method of solution 1, without explanations
sections.statement:
$$S=\alpha=13^{\mathrm h}29^{\mathrm m}56^{\mathrm s}=202.483^\circ=S_0+(T_c-8^{\mathrm h})\times(1+1/365.2422)+122.05^\circ,$$
$$S_0(^{\mathrm d})\approx93^{\mathrm d},\quad S_0(^\circ)=93^{\mathrm d}\times(360^\circ/365.2422^{\mathrm d})=91.67^\circ$$
$$\Rightarrow T_c=-11.2^\circ+120^\circ=108.8^\circ=7.25^{\mathrm h}=07^{\mathrm h}15^{\mathrm m}.$$
Answer: 07:15.

sections.title: 5.1. Method of solution 2, with explanations
sections.statement:
The upper culmination of a celestial body occurs when its sidereal time equals to its right ascension. It is ≈ 13ʰ30ᵐ for NGC 5194. Sidereal time is equal to mean solar time at the date of autumnal equinox, and then begins to outstrip it with speed 1ᵈ/365.2422 per day (about 3ᵐ56ˢ per day).

*Note. Strictly speaking, the sidereal time is equal to mean solar time about two days earlier, but we are not going to account for this subtle effect.*

93 days passed since September 22/23 (autumnal equinox) till December 24/25 (the observation was made). The difference between mean solar time and sidereal time at the night of observations is:
$$24^{\mathrm h}00^{\mathrm m}\times93^{\mathrm d}/365.2422^{\mathrm d}=6^{\mathrm h}07^{\mathrm m}$$
So on December 24/25 sidereal time 13ʰ30ᵐ corresponds to
$$13^{\mathrm h}30^{\mathrm m}-6^{\mathrm h}07^{\mathrm m}=7^{\mathrm h}23^{\mathrm m}\quad\text{of mean solar time.}$$
Weihai is located in 2.05° East from the meridian of 120° (base meridian for Beijing time UT+08), so the mean solar time here ahead the Beijing time by $2.05^\circ\times4^{\mathrm{m}/\circ}=8.2^{\mathrm m}\approx8^{\mathrm m}$. So to get answer according to time UT+08 we have to subtract these 8ᵐ, and we have
$$7^{\mathrm h}23^{\mathrm m}-0^{\mathrm h}08^{\mathrm m}=7^{\mathrm h}15^{\mathrm m}\quad\text{Beijing time.}$$
Answer: 07:15.
FoV = 2048 × 13.5 μm × 206265″ / 8 m = 712.85″ = 11.88′, so measured from the Figure, the angular size in diameter is β ≈ 55 mm / 116 mm × FoV ≈ 5.6′.
$$L=D/\beta(\mathrm{rad})\approx\tfrac12\times0.03\ \mathrm{Mpc}/(5.6'/3438^{\mathrm{rad}/'})\approx9\ \mathrm{Mpc}.$$
Type = spiral.
Find the Beijing time (UTC+08, write the answer in 24h format: hh:mm) of the upper culmination of NGC 5194 in Weihai Observatory on the observing date, in form of «$T_c=\ldots$».
Estimate the angular size (diameter) of NGC 5194 (in units of arc minutes, write the answer in form of «$\beta=\ldots$»).
If the physical size of NGC 5194 is known as about half the size of the Milky Way Galaxy, estimate the distance to M51 (in units of Mpc, write the answer in form of «$L=\ldots$»).
Which is the morphological type of NGC 5194 (“elliptical”, “spiral”, “barred spiral”, “irregular”)? Write the answer in English in form of «Type = ...».

problems.title: β-5. Seyfert galaxy.
problems.statement: The low-resolution spectrum of a galaxy: NGC 7479 ($\alpha=23^{\mathrm h}04^{\mathrm m}57^{\mathrm s}$, $\delta=+12^\circ19'22''$) was observed by the 2.16 m telescope of Xinglong Station near Beijing, National Astronomical Observatories of China, on September 14, 2009. The red part of this spectrum is shown in Fig.β5. (see separate sheet). The emission lines in the part of the spectrum are (from left to right): [NII]a, Hα, [NII]b.

figures.alt: Original NGC7479 spectrum with full wavelength, flux and emission-line labels

sections.title: 5.1. Method of solution 1, without explanations
sections.statement:
$$S=\alpha=23^{\mathrm h}04^{\mathrm m}57^{\mathrm s}=346.238^\circ=S_0+(T_c-8^{\mathrm h})\times(1+1/365.2422)+117.575^\circ,$$
$$S_0\approx-8^{\mathrm d}=-8^{\mathrm d}\times(360^\circ/365.2422^{\mathrm d})=-7.9^\circ$$
$$\Rightarrow T_c=-123.5^\circ+120^\circ=-3.5^\circ=-0.23^{\mathrm h}\ \to\ 23.77^{\mathrm h}=23^{\mathrm h}46^{\mathrm m}.$$
Answer: 23:46.

sections.title: 5.1. Method of solution 2, with explanations
sections.statement:
The upper culmination of a celestial body occurs when its sidereal time equals to its right ascension. It is ≈ 23ʰ05ᵐ for NGC 7479. Sidereal time is equal to mean solar time at the date of autumnal equinox, and then begins to outstrip it with speed 1ᵈ/365.2422 per day (about 3ᵐ56ˢ per day).

*Note. Strictly speaking, the sidereal time is equal to mean solar time about two days earlier, but we are not going to account for this subtle effect.*

8 days to be passed till September 22/23 (autumnal equinox) since September 14/15 (the observation was made). The difference between mean solar time and sidereal time at the night of observations is:
$$24^{\mathrm h}00^{\mathrm m}\times-8^{\mathrm d}/365.2422^{\mathrm d}=-31.5^{\mathrm m}$$
So on September 14/15 sidereal time 23ʰ05ᵐ corresponds to
$$23^{\mathrm h}05^{\mathrm m}-(-31.5^{\mathrm m})=23^{\mathrm h}36.5^{\mathrm m}\quad\text{of mean solar time.}$$
Xinglong Station is located in 2.425° West from the meridian of 120° (base meridian for Beijing time UT+08), so the mean solar time here behind the Beijing time by $2.425^\circ\times4^{\mathrm{m}/\circ}=9.7^{\mathrm m}\approx10^{\mathrm m}$. So to get answer according to time UT+08 we have to add these 9.7ᵐ ≈ 10ᵐ, and we have
$$23^{\mathrm h}36.5^{\mathrm m}+0^{\mathrm h}09.7^{\mathrm m}=23^{\mathrm h}46.2^{\mathrm m}\approx23^{\mathrm h}46^{\mathrm m}\quad\text{Beijing time.}$$
Answer: 23:46.

Maximum of the Hα emission line is observed at λobs = 6614 Å, while its laboratory wavelength is known as λ₀ = 6563 Å. So the redshift of NGC 7479 is
$$z=(\lambda_\mathrm{obs}-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0=(6614\ \text{Å}-6563\ \text{Å})/6563\ \text{Å}=51\ \text{Å}/6563\ \text{Å}\approx0.0078.$$
*Note. Real value from literature is z = 0.007935 ± 0.000017.*
$$D=v/H_0=zc/H_0=0.0078\times300000\ \mathrm{km/s}/68\ \mathrm{Mpc/(km/s)}\approx34\ \mathrm{Mpc}.$$

Measured from the spectrum, FWHM(Hα) = 10 Å, so in units of km/s,
$$\mathrm{FWHM}(\mathrm H\alpha)=10\ \text{Å}/6563\ \text{Å}\times300000\ \mathrm{km/s}\approx460\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$
Type = Seyfert-II.

Estimate the redshift z of this galaxy (write the answer in form of «$z=\ldots$»).

Estimate the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the Hα line (in units of km/s, write the answer in the form of «FWHM(Hα) = ...»).

If the galaxy is known as a Seyfert galaxy, based on the line width of Hα, which type it should be (“Seyfert-I” or “Seyfert-II”)? Write the answer in English in form of «Type = ...». (Assume that the instrumental broadening can be neglected.)
